historic_survey.survey: Inner Mission North Context Statement, adopted 2004
historic_survey.note: Named in the survey's Mission Historic Entertainment theme as the Alhambra Theater (Grand), covering public entertainment structures on 16th Street and on Mission Street from 16th to 25th Streets.
The Grand Theater, designed by G. Albert Lansburgh in 1940 — named as one of the few large commercial buildings built in the Streamline Moderne style.

historical_record.description: Before the theater, the site held a one-story building with five shopfronts.
A Russian-run barber shop traded here in 1939.
The building permit for the new theater was issued, filed under 2671 Mission Street.
The Grand Theater, 1940, by G. Albert Lansburgh, who turned from Classical and Eclectic work to the Streamline Moderne in the 1930s.

The Grand Theater went up as a one-story Streamline Moderne movie house of about 75 by 122.5 feet with two small shops, built for the Robert A. Lurie Co. (Peoples Theater Company) at a permitted cost of $44,700.
Theater operator D.B. Levin took a 99-year lease from the Lurie Co. to run the new theater, which cost about $250,000 to build and fit out; the Levin family ran it for many years.
The Grand opened as a family movie house for the Mission, the last movie theater built in San Francisco before World War II; it seated about 870 on a single raked floor.
Fire-insurance mapping showed the theater at 2665 Mission flanked by small stores at 2663 and 2671, built of reinforced concrete and steel with steel trusses.
In the 1950s one of the small shops was a candy store, possibly doubling as the theater's concession stand.
Photographed, showing the Grand Theater.
Like other Mission District cinemas, the Grand switched to Spanish-language films in the 1970s and 1980s.
Robert Durden photographed the property, showing Grand Theater.
The Grand closed as a movie theater, one of the last cinemas still running on Mission Street.
A permit converted the old theater into two shops: the raked floor was built up level, the screen removed, the proscenium walled in and a dividing wall run down the auditorium.
Robert Durden photographed the property, showing Grand Theater.
The Grand Theater, one of two Mission District cinemas showing Filipino films in the 1970s.
The Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board recommended starting landmark designation of the Grand Theater.
The Planning Commission voted against making the Grand Theater a landmark.
On appeal, the Board of Supervisors upheld the Planning Commission's refusal to designate the theater a landmark.
A permit removed the dividing wall to make one large retail space; the old ticket booth was gone by then.

The digital-arts nonprofit Grey Area renovated the building before moving in, adding a two-story interior block at the back of the auditorium and uncovering and restoring the proscenium; most of the lobby transom was filled in.
The partly restored neon on the tower sign was switched on, lighting the letters G-R-A-N-D for the first time in over 30 years.
The Board of Supervisors voted to start landmark designation of the Grand Theater, this time successfully.
The Historic Preservation Commission recommended the Grand Theater for landmark designation after a public hearing.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 315, Grand Theater.

unknowns: The Modern design context statement gives the Grand Theater three different street numbers — 2665, 2671 and 2761 Mission Street.
